title: Ezekiel 20:45–49
context: The LORD’s word comes to Ezekiel again, telling him to set his face toward the south and prophesy against the forest of the field in the south. The LORD will kindle a fire that devours every green and dry tree, unquenched, so that all flesh will see that the LORD has kindled it. The image is explained in the next chapter, where the south becomes Jerusalem, its sanctuaries, and the land of Israel (21:2). Ezekiel responds, Ah Lord GOD, because the people dismiss him as a speaker of parables (compare 17:2). In the Hebrew text, English 20:45–49 is numbered 21:1–5, and English 21:1–32 is numbered 21:6–37. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage as shared ground about the seriousness of God’s judgment and the burden of a prophet whose message is brushed aside.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s word coming to Ezekiel again. A new message begins, one that will be explained in the next chapter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet receiving another word from God. Readers in both traditions commonly note that this verse opens a new section that continues into the next chapter.

verses.text: “Son of man, set your face toward the south, and preach toward the south, and prophesy against the forest of the field in the south.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD telling Ezekiel to set his face toward the south and prophesy against the forest of the field. The image is ominous.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a prophetic image whose meaning will be explained in 21:2. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a parable of coming judgment.

verses.text: Tell the forest of the south, ‘Hear the LORD’s word: The Lord GOD says, “Behold, I will kindle a fire in you, and it will devour every green tree in you, and every dry tree. The burning flame will not be quenched, and all faces from the south to the north will be burned by it.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD kindling an unquenchable fire that consumes green and dry trees alike. Judgment will be sweeping.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image of a fire that no one can stop. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, in light of its explanation in the next chapter.

verses.text: All flesh will see that I, the LORD, have kindled it. It will not be quenched.” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see that all flesh will see that the LORD has kindled the fire. His hand in judgment will be evident to everyone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty openly displayed. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that judgment reveals who the LORD is.

verses.text: Then I said, “Ah Lord GOD! They say of me, ‘Isn’t he a speaker of parables?’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezekiel crying out, Ah Lord GOD, because the people dismiss him as a speaker of parables. His message is not being heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet’s burden when people brush off God’s word (compare Matthew 13:13). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with sympathy for the prophet.
